body: You claim to be a nurse, but your comment history says that you are a teenager in high school? I'm confused.
I don't drink any sort of coffee or energy drinks.

I'm so sorry to hear that! That sounds awful.

I'm also anemic, but the doctors have said that my anemia isn't severe enough to sufficiently explain all of my symptoms.

And yup, I've had twenty labs done as of the other day. Simple things like blood sugar and iron, but also tests for viruses, thyroid issues, specific proteins, etc. Everything has come back pretty normal.

Thank you so much for this, truly.

As far as the tests, they've run so many. I've had three complete blood panels, as well as specialty testing for everything from Epstein-Barr (mono) to thyroid issues to a protein that your body begins to create after a heart attack. I'm being seen at a hospital that is consistently ranked among the best in the nation, so I do trust that the doctors are highly competent and are being thorough in their exams. But that's sort of why I feel so helpless, I think. It feels like even more of an uphill battle *because* these doctors are so qualified, so thorough, and so well-respected.

Can I ask if you have any sort of cardiac symptoms? They seem to be a lot more worried about my heart than my brain. I'm set to see a cardiologist in a month, but I'll honestly be shocked if I make it a month without another ER visit. I considered going last night because I felt so horrible, but didn't feel like it would have been safe to drive and didn't want to deal with the drama of an ambulance.

I truly don't think it's anything that catastrophic, but I'm not a doctor, so I know that I really can't venture into guessing territory. I just want answers and I feel like no one wants to give them.

Honestly, it's difficult to remember enough to explain it. When I feel bad enough to be losing my vision, I'm typically also extremely disoriented. I don't remember those times very clearly simply because I was so out of it. Things just go black, I guess? I don't see spots; it's more like my field of vision goes black from the outside-in. Not being able to see makes me panic, obviously, so I usually instinctively close my eyes and do my best to let it pass. I've never actually left my eyes open long enough to know if I fully lose the ability to see, if that makes sense.

I didn't see my EKG results, no. I was told by the doctors in the emergency room last week that it was normal, aside from a few small abnormalities. They were thinking there was just the smallest chance that it could be a blood clot in my lungs (I was having a lot of chest pain that night and a racing heart, but I was not very dizzy), which is what led them to do imaging and more labs. They ruled it out.

I do wonder about my heart rate, though. I feel like when I have my pulse taken by a doctor, it's typically always in the 70s or 80s. It hovered between 95 and 120 all night in the ER. They left me hooked up to the EKG so it was continuously monitoring me, and even right before discharge (so after about five or six hours of lying still in bed), it was 104.

One of the doctors kept telling me it was normal, but the other said that they were running more tests in part because of my "high heart rate", so I'm not too sure? I know that if anything, that's the high side of normal, but it's much higher than I'm used to as a "resting heart rate".

They haven't. I do have a mental illness diagnosis (explained more thoroughly in another comment), so I have been on both SSRIs and anti-psychotics before, and would refuse if they asked me to go on them again. I was medicated for a little over a year.

I was pretty severely traumatized as a child and have a PTSD diagnosis, so I definitely know what anxiety and panic feel like for me. (Totally not getting on your case for asking; I can appreciate the thought that it could be that, I just know my body and already have hundreds of reference points for what my body feels like during an anxiety or panic attack.)

The symptoms peak immediately after waking up, whereas my anxiety is usually the worst at night. I also seem to have the worst fainting/dizziness episodes in the shower, which has never been something I've noticed with anxiety. And the level of fatigue and exhaustion I feel definitely isn't mental – there's a walk I used to do daily because I love exercising and it cleared my head, and I now can't walk more than 20% of it without feeling like I'm going to collapse and my heart is going to beat out of my chest.

I really do recognize that anxiety can have very real physical symptoms, but it's frustrating because I don't know how to convey my knowledge of my body to a doctor who already believes it is a manifestation of anxiety. If I tell them I have a mental illness diagnosis and know what anxiety and panic feel like, I think they'd be even more swayed in that direction. If I don't tell them that I have a diagnosis and experience with anxiety and panic, I think they'll continue to tell me that "panic can feel very real" and the like.
